name: El Salvador International Airport Saint Óscar Arnulfo Romero y Galdámez
before:
El Salvador's international gateway, and third in Central America for passenger movements at around 3.4 million a year. It is a joint civilian and military field in San Luis Talpa, in the south of the country.

The transfer is better than the distance suggests. A four lane motorway runs the 42 km into San Salvador and the drive averages about thirty minutes, which is quick for a capital this far from its airport.

The setting is unusual: a triangle of ground with the Pacific on its southern boundary and the Jiboa River to the east. Being close to sea level, aircraft can operate at full capacity rather than being weight limited, which matters for long haul routes out of Central America.

It carries FAA category 1 status. The airport is now named after Saint Oscar Arnulfo Romero y Galdamez, having previously been Comalapa International, so both names still appear on schedules and in supplier systems.
after:
El Salvador's main international airport sits in San Luis Talpa, just over 30 km south east of San Salvador in a straight line. It handled more than 5.2 million passengers in 2025, according to its operator, CEPA.

Its full name honours Saint Óscar Arnulfo Romero y Galdámez, but it is usually called El Salvador International Airport, and it was previously known as Comalapa International.

The US FAA gives El Salvador its Category 1 safety rating, which covers the country's oversight of aviation rather than the airport itself.

claims.inAfter: The US FAA gives El Salvador its Category 1 safety rating, which covers the country's oversight of aviation rather than the airport itself.
claims.note: Was 'It carries FAA category 1 status', as if the airport were rated. The FAA's IASA programme rates a country's civil aviation safety oversight against ICAO standards, not an airport or an airline; its current results table (dated 18 April 2025, read 23 September 2026) lists El Salvador as Category 1. Wikipedia repeats the airport wording.

claims.claim: the transfer is better than the distance suggests; four lane motorway; 42 km; about thirty minutes
claims.wasBefore: The transfer is better than the distance suggests. A four lane motorway runs the 42 km into San Salvador and the drive averages about thirty minutes, which is quick for a capital this far from its airport.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone, and it disagrees with itself: its lead gives a four-lane motorway, 42 km and 30 minutes, its infrastructure section 'about 50 km (31 mi) by road'. Both distances pass the coordinates check, so neither can be chosen. Its source for the lead appears to be the old airport site (aeropuertoelsalvador.gob.sv), which survives only in the web archive (blocked by the network policy); CEPA's airport page, FAQ and history give no distance or time, and El Salvador's tourism site had no page on getting from the airport. The straight-line distance is kept (above); 'better than the distance suggests' and 'quick for a capital' are judgements that fall with the facts.

claims.claim: direct flights to Madrid
claims.why: Held back: the civil aviation authority (AAC) marked Avianca's relaunch of the direct San Salvador to Madrid route on 13 June 2026, and CEPA announced on 1 August 2026 that Air Europa will start direct San Salvador to Madrid flights in December 2026. The AAC also says Iberojet has announced Madrid and Barcelona routes (a headline only; that page was not saved). Useful to a UK agent, but the old text names no airline or route, so there is nothing to replace. For Andy to decide.

claims.claim: FCDO: entry, transit fee and taxis
claims.why: Held back, for the record: the FCDO says British visitors can stay up to 180 days without a visa; Indian nationals and nationals of any African country travelling through El Salvador must pay a 1,130 US dollar fee (British dual nationals travelling on a British passport do not); and for short trips it advises radio-dispatched, pre-booked or hotel taxis, never unofficial ones. The state of exception declared in 2022 is still in place. Nothing in the old text to replace.

quote: You can travel to El Salvador for tourism or business for up to 180 days without a visa.
Indian nationals or nationals from any African country travelling through El Salvador must pay a 1,130 US dollar fee.
For shorter trips within towns and cities, take radio-dispatched, pre-booked or hotel taxis operated by reputable companies. Do not use unofficial taxis, as there remains a small risk of kidnapping.
The state of exception started in 2022 and has remained in place since.
